description: The workspace webview shows the ship-served lattice client (any user-configured URL, so the pattern is any host), so everything here is reachable by whatever the ship serves and each grant is justified on that basis. pick_upload, save_vault and pick_vault all open a native dialog and act ONLY on what the user then picks: a hostile page gets nothing without a visible OS dialog and a deliberate choice in it. open_external_url sends target=_blank links (the clearweb share link) to the system browser, refusing anything outside http, https, mailto and tel, enforced in rust rather than in the page. backup_write takes bytes for an EXISTING schedule id only; the page cannot choose the directory or the filename, both come from the stored schedule, and the schedule's own retention bounds how many files it can leave behind. NOTE: save_vault and pick_vault were missing here until the scheduled-backup work, which meant vault export and restore in the desktop app failed on 'not allowed. Command not found' — deny-by-default is right, but a command the client calls and never gets is a feature that silently does not exist. The queue-* commands back the offline queue and are called ONLY by the ship's own client, which is also the only thing that can produce an edit to queue. They read and write a per-ship directory under the app's data dir; a hostile page could fill that directory with junk it invented, which is bounded and visible, and is a far smaller risk than the alternative on the table — no offline queue at all, and edits lost every time the ship is unreachable. pandoc_probe and convert_tex were missing here for exactly the same reason save_vault and pick_vault were, and failed the same way: the button reported that pandoc was not installed on a machine where it was. Both are safe to grant. pandoc_probe runs `pandoc --version` and returns whether it worked, taking no argument from the page at all. convert_tex pipes the page’s own text through pandoc on stdin and returns the html, choosing the binary itself and never taking a path or a flag from the caller, so a hostile page can spend cpu converting its own text and nothing more.
